item.content:encoded:
Views: 25

Contributed by Dan Rose, a Senior Local Business Guide Specializing in Personal Injury Legal Services in New York City

Ask anyone in Forest Hills who has been in a collision and you will hear the same worry, usually phrased as an apology. I think I was a little bit at fault. They were pulling out of a parking spot on Austin Street. They stepped off the curb at Yellowstone Boulevard a second before the signal changed. They were riding along the Queens Boulevard service road without a helmet.

For fifty years that admission cost a New Yorker some money but never the case itself. As of this year, in car accident claims, it can cost the case. The rule changed in May, quietly, as part of the state budget, and most people hurt on Queens streets have no idea it happened.

What New York used to do, and why it was unusual

New York has been a pure comparative fault state since 1975. Under CPLR 1411, a jury decided how responsible each side was and reduced the award accordingly, with no cutoff. A driver found 80 percent responsible for her own injuries still collected 20 percent of her damages. Most states stop that at 50 or 51 percent. New York did not, and for five decades that made it one of the most claimant-friendly states in the country on this one question.

What the 2026 amendment says

Part EE of Chapter 58 of the Laws of 2026 was signed on May 26, 2026. It added a new subdivision, CPLR 1411(b), which bars recovery where the fault attributable to the claimant is greater than the fault of the party being sued. In plain terms: 50 percent and you still recover half; 51 percent and you recover nothing.

Three limits on that sentence matter more than the sentence does.

It only reaches motor vehicle cases. Subdivision (b) applies to actions subject to article 51 of the Insurance Law, which is the no-fault article. A fall on an icy stairwell in a Forest Hills co-op, a dog bite in Forest Park, a construction injury on Queens Boulevard — all of those remain governed by CPLR 1411(a), unchanged, pure comparative. A claimant 70 percent at fault in one of those still recovers 30 percent.

It runs from the filing date, not the crash date. The amendments apply to actions commenced on or after May 26, 2026. A collision from 2024 or 2025 that has not yet been filed is governed by the new rule. People assume the law that applies is the law on the day they were hurt. Here it is not.

Where pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists sit is not settled. Article 51 was written around insured motor vehicles and their occupants. Whether a pedestrian struck on Queens Boulevard is in an action “subject to” that article is a question the courts have not answered, and anyone telling a cyclist confidently one way or the other in 2026 is guessing.

Fault is something the other side has to prove

This is the part that gets lost, and it is the most useful thing in this article.

Comparative fault is not a hole you have to climb out of. Under CPLR 1412 it is an affirmative defense, which means the party asserting it has to plead it and prove it. The insurer does not get to assign you a percentage over the phone and have that be the number. Its lawyer has to convince a jury of it, with evidence, and if the evidence is thin the percentage comes down.

The Court of Appeals underlined the point in Rodriguez v City of New York, 31 NY3d 312, decided in 2018. A plaintiff does not have to prove the absence of his own comparative fault in order to win on liability. Fault and damages are separate questions, argued separately, and being partly responsible does not stop you from establishing that the other driver was responsible too.

How a percentage actually gets decided

Juries do not pick numbers out of the air. They are pointed at specific rules of the road and asked who broke which one. A rear-end collision on the Queens Boulevard service road runs into Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1129(a), which says a driver “shall not follow another vehicle more closely than is reasonable and prudent.” That is why the following driver starts the argument behind. A pedestrian case at a crosswalk runs into § 1151, which requires drivers to yield but also says no pedestrian “shall suddenly leave a curb or other place of safety and walk or run into the path of a vehicle.” Both halves of that section get read to the jury.

On top of the statutes sit the physical facts: signal timing, camera footage, the position of the damage, what the responding officer wrote down, and what witnesses remember. In a place like Forest Hills, where Queens Boulevard carries twelve lanes past three subway entrances, those details are usually available for a short while and then gone.

It is worth noting that the street itself has changed. The city’s own figures for the redesigned stretch of Queens Boulevard between Roosevelt Avenue and Eliot Avenue showed pedestrian injuries falling from an average of 40.3 a year to 18 after the work was done, a 55 percent drop. Safer does not mean safe, and it does not settle who was at fault on any given morning.

Four things insurers call fault that the law does not

Adjusters raise these constantly. It is worth knowing which ones have statutory teeth and which are noise.

You were not wearing a seat belt. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1229-c(8) says non-compliance “shall not be admissible as evidence in any civil action … in regard to the issue of liability,” though it may be introduced in mitigation of damages if it was pleaded as an affirmative defense. So it can reduce what you collect for the injuries the belt would have prevented. It cannot make the crash your fault.

You were on a bicycle without a helmet. New York requires helmets for riders under fourteen and for operators of class three e-bikes. For everyone else there is no requirement, and VTL § 1238(7) is unusually direct about the consequence: failure to comply “shall not constitute contributory negligence or assumption of risk, and shall not in any way bar, preclude or foreclose an action for personal injury or wrongful death.”

You did not go to the hospital that day. This is not fault at all. It is an argument about whether the injury came from the crash, which is a different fight, though a real one — whether your injuries clear New York’s serious injury threshold is a separate test with its own rules, and it turns entirely on what ends up in your medical file.

You do not have a license, or you are not documented. Neither bears on whether the other driver ran the light. Immigration status is not a defense to negligence in New York, and a claim should never be abandoned over it.

What this looks like with numbers

A teacher leaves the 71st–Continental Avenue station and crosses Queens Boulevard at the signal. A driver turning from the service road strikes her. She had stepped off maybe a second early. The insurer puts 30 percent on her.

Suppose the case is worth $200,000. At 30 percent she recovers $140,000, and the new rule changes nothing, because 30 is not greater than 70. Now suppose the driver’s lawyer builds a better record — a witness who says she was looking at her phone, a signal timing chart — and the jury comes back at 55 percent. Under the old law she takes home $90,000. Under the law as it stands today she takes home nothing.

The gap between those two outcomes is $90,000, and it is decided by 5 percentage points of fault. That is why the fight over the percentage, which used to be a fight about how much, is now sometimes a fight about whether.

Where these cases go wrong

Apologizing at the scene

“I’m so sorry, I didn’t see you” is what decent people say when someone is hurt in front of them. It also goes into the police report and gets read back years later as an admission. Check on people, call 911, exchange information, and leave the fault analysis to people who were not standing in traffic.

Giving the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement

You must cooperate with your own no-fault carrier. You are under no obligation to be interviewed by the other side’s. Those calls come within days, they are friendly, and the questions are built to produce percentages.

Assuming a shared-fault case is not worth bringing

Plenty of people hear “you were partly at fault” and stop. If the split is anywhere at or below even, the claim still exists, and the split is an argument, not a finding. Under CPLR 1412 nobody has proved anything until the defense does.

Letting the scene evidence disappear

Percentages get argued from signal timing, camera footage, skid marks and witnesses. Business cameras along Austin Street and the Queens Boulevard service roads generally overwrite within days or weeks. A lawyer who sends a preservation letter in week one is protecting the percentage, which is now protecting the case.

Waiting because the crash was a while ago

Because the new rule attaches to the filing date, an older claim that has not been filed is already living under it. That is a reason to get the file in front of someone now rather than at the end of the three-year limitations period.

Common questions

Does this apply to my slip and fall?
No. The bar in CPLR 1411(b) is limited to actions subject to the no-fault article. Premises cases, dog bites and construction accidents stay pure comparative, where even a mostly responsible claimant recovers a share.

The insurer already told me I was 60 percent at fault. Is that it?
No. That is a position, not a determination. Comparative fault has to be pleaded and proved by the party asserting it, and adjusters open high on purpose.

My accident was in 2024 and I never filed. Which rule applies?
The new one, because the amendments attach to actions commenced on or after May 26, 2026. This is the single most common misunderstanding about the change.

I was hit while walking. Am I covered by this?
Unsettled, and anyone who says otherwise is ahead of the courts. Article 51 was drafted around motor vehicles and their occupants, and the question of how a pedestrian’s claim sits inside it has not been decided.

Can I be found at fault for a crash I did not cause?
Partly, yes — speed, distraction, a missed signal or an unsafe lane change can each carry a share even when the other driver caused the collision. The share is what is worth arguing about.

This article is general information about New York law and not legal advice. Reading it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Every claim depends on its own facts, and the law described here was accurate as of September 2026.

Speak to a Queens injury attorney

If you were hurt in Forest Hills, Rego Park, Kew Gardens or anywhere else in the borough and someone has suggested the crash was partly your doing, that is a reason to get advice sooner rather than later, not a reason to let it go. Consultations cost nothing and there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

item.content:encoded:
Views: 39

QueensWay with preserved historic railroad infrastructure.

BY MICHAEL PERLMAN

mperlman@queensledger.com

“Hop aboard the QueensWay!”… Not to catch a train, since trains were last decommissioned from the LIRR Rockaway Beach Branch Line in 1962 due to minimal passenger counts and fire damage, but for Queens’ first linear park and cultural greenway of its kind. The QueensWay will be stationed along an abandoned route, such as where a Forest Hills trestle on Metropolitan Avenue bears a stone inscription of 1908. Fast-forwarding, late 2026 will mark the groundbreaking of the QueensWay’s construction, complete with community leaders driving shovels into the soil alongside a lush forested but long-neglected industrial backdrop for phase 1, the Metropolitan Hub.

Volunteer opportunities are plentiful and can be found on the QueensWay’s social media and Trust For Public Land’s website. A public cleanup of the QueensWay in Forest Park will be held on September 27 at 10:30 AM (meet at Stop & Shop), and the QueensWay 5K 2026 will be on October 4 at 9 AM at Victory Field.

Enter the world of 35-year-old John Surico, a 12-year Astoria resident and former Floral Park resident, who has his heart throughout Queens, beating in the direction of its future while celebrating its past. This adds to last week’s column, which focused on the QueensWay’s status and goals, as well as the background of Friends of the QueensWay’s board member, Karen Imas of Forest Hills. Surico is an outstanding voice in urbanism and a largely respected writer, researcher, and organizer, who prioritizes mobility and open space. As September rolled in, he made history as Friends of the QueensWay’s first executive director, which is his dream come true.

The QueensWay will ultimately bridge the Central and Southern Queens communities of Rego Park, Forest Hills, Woodhaven, Glendale, Richmond Hill, and Ozone Park, and also anchor Queens enthusiasts through recreation, the arts, cultural foods, and historic and environmental preservation. It also bridges historically disconnected residential areas. A much-needed green space will feature current and new diverse trees, native vegetation, and edible gardens. A pedestrian and bike path will offer a newly commanding bird’s-eye exposure of neighborhoods, and enable access to nearby bike lanes en route to Rockaway Beach and Jamaica Bay’s recreational spaces, as well as five subway lines, numerous commercial corridors, and schools.

Back in 2011, Queens residents living alongside the abandoned LIRR Rockaway Beach Branch had an ambitious vision for the 3.5-mile stretch, joined forces, and began advocating for its revitalization into a vibrant yet serene public park. This grassroots initiative led to the creation of Friends of the QueensWay, a community-driven organization supported by hundreds of individuals and groups through petitions, fundraisers, cleanups, tours, and events.

In recent times, Surico served as Senior Fellow for Climate and Opportunity at the Center for an Urban Future, and drew his energy towards parks and open space. “I led their parks portfolios and focused on research reports and policy recommendations on how to improve the parks of New York City, and acquire more funding. It was through that work, the QueensWay was placed on my radar,” said Surico.

For 10+ years, he has provided coverage of parks among public spaces as a journalist. For over five years in Astoria, Surico has been a strong advocate for public space, and proudly became the Chair of 31st Avenue Open Street Collective. He explained, “It is a pop-up space on weekends, where on two blocks we introduce tons of free programming, including performances, have long tables of outdoor seating, and partner with local businesses for events. That exposed me to the need for thriving public space, engagement, programming reflective of the community, and building up a volunteer effort in 2020 with few people to a nonprofit with 100+ volunteers and 100+ programmers.” This enabled him to work with elected officials and help introduce additional permanent public space to Western Queens, which ranks upwards of the lesser ten of council districts for the lack of public space. Additionally, he serves as a board member of the Alliance for Flushing Meadows Corona Park.

“For much of my work early on, I was in touch with Trust For Public Land, which plays a pivotal role in the QueensWay,” said Surico. That entails engagement and elected official support. “I wrote about the QueensWay and visited then. To make history as QueensWay’s first executive director is unbelievable. I could not have imagined it a couple of years ago. It has been an exciting project, specifically since we do not have many projects like it in NYC. It is unique in terms of where it is and what existed. It is quite different from the High Line. Being able to do a project in the borough that I live in is really exciting,” he continued.

Surico explained his vision for The QueensWay. “As someone who has a family history in Queens and knows the navigational disconnect between the neighborhoods that it would serve, it is a tremendous opportunity to link them through walking, running, biking, and open space. I want to show people that it is possible and have New Yorkers reimagine the space.” Surico, who views historic photos, finds this rare redevelopment opportunity intriguing, and marvels over how the route has been abandoned for decades, causing trees to grow between the rails. “Let’s think about the diverse benefits; not only recreational space, especially for the Metropolitan Expeditionary Learning School, but rewilding the space with amazing biodiversity, adding stormwater retention (flooding has been on the rise in recent years), and making it accessible to all. Let’s also make it accessible for all these neighborhoods as a backyard to put on programming, and I am really excited about that potential.”

In the short-term, his goal is lifting much of the work from the plate of volunteers over the years and centralizing the initiative. “The fact that Karen Imas and the rest of the board have pursued this in their free time is admirable. Let’s determine everyone’s roles and what we can focus on, including which kinds of fundraisers and volunteer engagements we can coordinate. The question becomes, ‘What’s a one-stop shop where everyone can see what’s going on with the QueensWay? Where are places we can pop up to tell people what’s happening?”

As for a long-term goal, he said, “Once construction starts, I will be the eyes on the ground and want to be a trusted messenger to all businesses along Metropolitan Avenue. I will be an on-the-ground liaison for all community residents. I plan to potentially bring on additional staff and would love to have a benefit in the next calendar year.” His goal is to determine how the organization can assure that once the QueensWay opens, routine maintenance, programming, and safety protocols will be in place to live up to the envisioned world-class amazing park.

With a background in communication and engagement, Surico is ideal for the QueensWay’s promotional factor. “Before becoming an executive director, I would see what’s going on along Austin Street, at Forest Hills Stadium, Metropolitan Avenue, as well as along other parts of the rail, such as Ozone Park and Richmond Hill,” he said. His eyes are open to upcoming tabling events that he and his team can participate in, as well as citywide tour dates that would be ideal for parties of interest to become acquainted with the QueensWay. He is also on the lookout for presentation opportunities, press conferences, and becoming a panelist at diverse events. He visualizes presenting at Community Board 6 and the Forest Hills Greenmarket. Friends of the QueensWay will continue to be a dynamic force with the Trust For Public Land.

The route’s history, ambiance, and its potential inspires Surico, who estimates two to three years for completing phase 1 of the QueensWay. “These are the backyards my parents grew up in. My mom grew up in City Line, just below Forest Park, and my dad was raised in Ozone Park. I’ve been going to Eddie’s Sweet Shop and Aigner Chocolates since I was a kid. To be able to do a project here feels like a higher-level fate. The potential is remarkable for this long-abandoned stretch of land in our backyard that the city wanted nothing to do with. I have been heartened by a number of the design elements that the city put forward so far in its presentations, which bears homage to its history, such as reusing some of the rail and steel infrastructure. I will keep an eye on how to highlight artifacts. Karen Imas and the team have been using the term ‘cultural greenway,’ which not only shows what came before, but the future.” He noted other rail lines that have been abandoned in New York, such as the High Line, which the public helped repurpose into a major destination.

John Surico, New Executive Director of Friends of the QueensWay.

Surico feels that the ambiance of being able to create a transporting place behind busy commercial and vehicular corridors, and have a refuge and hub of activity, has been essential for the team to translate to partners. Additionally, he explained, “The history of residents and their advocacy behind this project for a long time has been amazing to watch. I have been learning a lot about that local community.”

Cleanups and tours influence attendees to imagine the QueensWay’s potential, which will bring nature to the forefront. The QueensWay’s stretch will border Forest Park, which is among the most idyllic destinations citywide for migratory birds besides Jamaica Bay, according to Surico, who goes birding. Such events are periodic. “Some of our earliest supporters were the birding community and hikers, since they would come upon this rail and say, ‘What is this?’ You have an opportunity to improve the route with more parkland for wildlife species to go, and reintroduce local native trees and pollinators.” He commended the Forest Park Trust and explained that what exists can be enhanced and expanded upon.

The EDC’s presentation provides hints of graceful to flamboyant species of trees and plants, which will be introduced. Some consist of Shadblow Serviceberry, known for its white blooms in the spring and feeding birds all summer long, as well as Tulip Trees, where tulip-shaped flowers peak after decades, and the deciduous trees are regarded as North America’s tallest. Eastern Redbud is praised for its energy, where abundant pink blooms are first to take wing. Then there is Red Maple, which Friends of the QueensWay stated, “Goes full flame every October. The one photo everyone reposts.” Taylor Eastern Red Cedar is a majestic evergreen.

Diverse plants will include Staghorn Sumac, recognized as “The drama queen. Goes full crimson every October like it’s got somewhere to be.” As for Oakleaf Hydrangea, they stated, “Already booked for every corridor selfie. No notes.” Making our way to New Jersey Tea, it is referenced for its fireworks depiction. “Works like one too, where every pollinator in the block shows up,” stated Friends of the QueensWay. It is known that the birds will quarrel over Elderberry plants. Inkberry is praised for remaining green in February. “Somebody on this corridor has to,” they stated.

“One of my first short-term goals is devising a volunteer set of touchpoints for upcoming events, such as cleanups and landscaping, and other forms of engagement,” said Surico, who encounters an audience that wishes to lend a helping hand. “There are so many people who want to help, so how do you tap into local talent?” he asked.

One of his immediate major focuses besides the construction of the QueensWay’s phase 1, the Metropolitan Hub, will be promotions. Surico explained, “Phase 1 will be an existential moment, since it shows people that the project is still happening. There will be such a powerful message once we get the shovels in the ground. Then we need to acquire additional political and institutional support for funds for the next phases. Once phase 1 is underway, we can gain momentum. Borough President Donovan Richards recently visited and said, ‘This is the year of the QueensWay.’ He committed to funding a little more of an expansion further south into Forest Park during phase 1, which would be really exciting.”

Volunteer cleanup along the QueensWay.

Phase 1 will be somewhat more than a half a mile, which accounts for a little less than a third of the QueensWay’s total length. That phase would currently span from Metropolitan Avenue behind Trader Joe’s and the Metropolitan Expeditionary Learning School to Union Turnpike. “I feel it is really important for New Yorkers to see that there are improvements being made where they live. Queens residents felt like other parts of our city are receiving more attention, but now we will have a world-class, first of its kind project,” he said.

When Surico is not focusing on the QueensWay, he is always exploring the beautiful borough of Queens, leading park and tree pit cleanups, becoming acquainted with diverse foods, and enjoying travel. In response to Queens’ nickname as “The World’s Borough,” he said, “We will determine different ways to introduce programming along the QueensWay to reflect diverse culture.”

The QueensWay will offer a multi-generational, exploratory, and neighborly experience. Some residents recall the route’s past as a rail. “It’s crazy for me, since I live with a parent who remembers when it was a rail when he was a kid. I spoke to my father all about this. He can’t even imagine what it would be like as a park, but he has been to other parts of the city that were transformed in his lifetime,” said Surico. The commendable and dynamic team is committed towards developing a momentous destination that is part of a larger picture of a more equitable and livable city. Queens is ready for a new chapter. To follow the cause and volunteer, visit www.thequeensway.org

item.dc:creator: BQE Admin

The post Spousal Maintenance in Queens: What Happens Between the Filing and the Final Judgment appeared first on This is Forest Hills.
item.content:encoded:
Views: 44

Contributed by Dan Rose, a Senior Local Business Guide Specializing in Family Law Services in New York City

Spousal maintenance in Queens usually arrives as two separate orders, not one, though most people filing for divorce expect a single number decided at the end. A temporary maintenance order runs while the case is pending, and a post-divorce maintenance award is set in the judgment — different sections of the statute, calculated at different moments, and frequently different numbers.

Understanding which one you are looking at, and when it gets decided, matters more than most people realize. A spouse who treats the first order as the final answer negotiates against a number that was never meant to last.

Two orders, two sections of the statute

Temporary maintenance comes from Domestic Relations Law § 236(B)(5-a). It applies while the action is pending and ends, by the statute’s own terms, no later than the issuance of the judgment of divorce or the death of either spouse, whichever comes first.

Post-divorce maintenance comes from § 236(B)(6). It takes over at the judgment and runs for whatever term the court sets.

The formulas look alike, which is why the two get confused. Both use the same arithmetic:

  • Where the payor also pays child support: 20% of the payor’s income minus 25% of the payee’s income; or 40% of combined income minus the payee’s income. The lower figure governs.
  • Where there is no child support, or the payor is the custodial parent: 30% of the payor’s income minus 20% of the payee’s income; or 40% of combined income minus the payee’s income. Again, the lower figure.

A zero or negative result means no guideline maintenance.

What differs is everything around the arithmetic. A temporary order is often decided on motion papers, early, before financial disclosure is complete. The post-divorce award is decided after discovery, with real documents in the file. Same formula, very different quality of input.

The number every calculation starts from: $241,000

The formulas apply to the payor’s income only up to a statutory cap. The statute itself writes that cap as $184,000 and directs that it rise every two years by the change in the consumer price index for all urban consumers, so the figure in the statute book is never the figure in use.

As of March 1, 2026, the maintenance income cap is $241,000, up from $228,000. The child support combined income cap moved to $193,000 in the same adjustment, and the self-support reserve to $21,546.

Income above the cap is not ignored. It is simply no longer automatic — the court may award more, in its discretion, after weighing the statutory factors: the length of the marriage, the ages and health of the spouses, present and future earning capacity, the need for education or training, the standard of living during the marriage, care of children or elderly relatives, and the rest of the list in the statute.

That distinction is where a lot of money changes hands in Queens, where a household with a business owner, a co-op, and two professional incomes can clear the cap without either spouse thinking of themselves as wealthy.

A Queens example, worked three ways

Take a couple in Forest Hills. One spouse earns $190,000. The other earns $55,000. The marriage has run twelve years.

No minor children. The no-child-support formula applies:

  • 30% of $190,000 = $57,000, minus 20% of $55,000 ($11,000) = $46,000
  • 40% of combined income ($245,000) = $98,000, minus $55,000 = $43,000

The lower figure governs: $43,000 a year, about $3,583 a month.

Same incomes, two children, payor is the non-custodial parent. Now the child-support formula applies:

  • 20% of $190,000 = $38,000, minus 25% of $55,000 ($13,750) = $24,250
  • 40% of $245,000 = $98,000, minus $55,000 = $43,000

The guideline drops to $24,250 a year, about $2,021 a month — and maintenance is calculated first, then subtracted from the payor’s income and added to the payee’s before child support is run. The payor’s income for the child support calculation becomes $165,750; the payee’s becomes $79,250.

Same household, payor earning $300,000. Only $241,000 of that income goes into the formula:

  • 30% of $241,000 = $72,300, minus $11,000 = $61,300
  • 40% of $296,000 = $118,400, minus $55,000 = $63,400

The guideline is $61,300. The payor’s income rose by 58%; the guideline rose by 43%. The remaining $59,000 of income is argued, not calculated.

How your income actually gets proved

The formula is only as good as the income figures fed into it, and those come from a sworn statement of net worth.

Under the uniform matrimonial rules (22 NYCRR 202.16(f)(1)), the statement must be exchanged and filed no later than ten days before the preliminary conference, and the conference itself is to be held within 45 days after the action is assigned. The statement does not travel alone. It comes with paycheck stubs for the current year and the last stub from the prior year, filed state and federal returns for the past three years, and W-2s, 1099s and K-1s for the same period.

In Queens, matrimonial filings go through the matrimonial office at the Jamaica courthouse (Room 140), and preliminary conferences are calendared in Room 5002 at 9:30 a.m. unless the court directs otherwise. Communication with the preliminary conference part is by email, with all parties copied.

A thin or late net worth statement is the single most common reason a maintenance fight drags. The other side gets an adjournment, the temporary order sits unchanged, and the spouse waiting on support waits longer.

When the court decides you earn more than you reported

Line 1 of a tax return is a starting point, not a conclusion. A court can impute income — treat a spouse as earning more than the return shows — where earnings were reduced without good reason, where compensation runs through a business, or where the lifestyle on display does not match the reported figure.

This comes up constantly in a borough built on small business. A restaurant owner in Rego Park, a contractor in Middle Village, a driver with 1099 income and a leased vehicle written off against it: in each case the deductions that are perfectly legitimate on a tax return may be added back for support purposes.

Imputation is evidentiary, not punitive. It has to be supported — bank deposits, credit card statements, the business’s own books — and a spouse who merely asserts that the other is hiding money, without the documents, usually loses that argument.

Where this goes wrong

Five failures account for most of the damage, and none of them are about the math.

The temporary order is treated as a preview

It is not one. It was decided early, on incomplete disclosure, under a different section of the statute, and it dies at the judgment. Settling the case around that figure — in either direction — is how a spouse ends up bound to a number that was never litigated.

Child support is run before maintenance

The statute sets the order of operations: maintenance is calculated first and moved from the payor’s income to the payee’s before child support. Reversing it inflates the child support figure and understates the maintenance figure, and the error survives into the judgment unless someone catches it.

The net worth statement goes in incomplete

Missing K-1s, no prior-year stub, three years of returns reduced to one. The immediate cost is delay. The longer cost is credibility, which is difficult to rebuild in front of a judge who has already been told the documents were coming.

Nobody argues the income above the cap

A guideline calculation on the first $241,000 is the floor, not the ceiling. Income above the cap is awarded only if someone puts the statutory factors in front of the court and asks. Silence gets treated as agreement.

Duration is left to default

The schedule is advisory, and the statute expressly permits non-durational maintenance in an appropriate case. A long marriage, a spouse who left the workforce, a serious health issue — these are duration arguments, and they are lost by not being made.

How long a final award runs

The advisory schedule keys duration to the length of the marriage:

  • Up to 15 years: 15% to 30% of the length of the marriage
  • More than 15 and up to 20 years: 30% to 40%
  • More than 20 years: 35% to 50%

For the twelve-year marriage in the example above, the advisory range is roughly 1.8 to 3.6 years of maintenance.

The statute defines the length of the marriage as the period from the date of marriage until the date the action was commenced — not the date the couple separated, a distinction that matters to anyone who lived apart for years before filing. And where the court departs from the guideline amount because it would be unjust or inappropriate, it has to state the unadjusted guideline figure, the factors it weighed and its reasons, either on the record or in a written decision.

Spouses can also opt out by agreement. To hold up, the agreement must be in writing, signed, and acknowledged the way a deed is acknowledged, and its terms must be fair and reasonable when made and not unconscionable at the time of judgment.

When the order stops being followed

Maintenance that is ordered and not paid becomes an arrears problem, and there are mechanisms for it. Unpaid support can be reduced to a money judgment for the arrears, and support obligations can be collected directly from wages through an income execution or an income deduction order under CPLR 5241 and 5242.

Going the other way, an order can be modified on a showing that the payee cannot be self-supporting, or on a substantial change in circumstances, including financial hardship or actual full or partial retirement. Where the obligation comes from an agreement rather than a court order, the bar is higher — extreme hardship.

One practical note: a change has to be real and continuing. A bad quarter is not a substantial change in circumstances.

What to do next

If you are at the beginning, get the financial documents together before the preliminary conference rather than after it — three years of returns, the stubs, the K-1s, the account statements. The quality of the temporary order depends almost entirely on what is in the file in the first sixty days.

If you already have a temporary order and the case is heading toward judgment, the question is whether the income figures behind it survived discovery. If they did not, the post-divorce calculation is where that gets corrected.

For a fuller walk-through of the guideline math itself — both formulas, the cap, and the factors the court weighs above it — the firm’s own explainer is here: how spousal maintenance is calculated in New York.

Frequently asked questions

How soon after filing can I get support?
Temporary maintenance is requested by motion and can be decided while the case is pending; in practice the timing follows the motion calendar and the preliminary conference, which is set within 45 days of assignment.

Does the temporary order carry over after the divorce is final?
No. Temporary maintenance ends no later than the judgment of divorce. Whatever continues after that is the post-divorce award, calculated separately.

My spouse is paid in cash. Is there anything I can do?
Yes, but it takes documents rather than assertions. Courts can impute income based on deposits, spending, and business records where reported income does not reflect what is actually available.

We agreed on a number ourselves. Will the court accept it?
It can, if the agreement is in writing, signed, and acknowledged like a deed, and the terms are fair and reasonable when made and not unconscionable at the time of judgment.

Can maintenance last for life?
It can. The durational schedule is advisory, and the statute specifically allows non-durational maintenance in an appropriate case, typically a long marriage or a spouse who cannot realistically become self-supporting.

This article describes New York law in general terms and is not legal advice. Maintenance outcomes depend on the facts of each marriage, and the statutory income caps are adjusted periodically.

item.content:encoded:
Views: 60

By Michael Perlman | mperlman@queensledger.com

“Hop aboard The QueensWay!”… Not to catch a train, since trains were last decommissioned from the LIRR Rockaway Beach Branch Line in 1962 due to minimal passenger counts and fire damage, but for the first linear park and cultural greenway of its kind in Queens. The QueensWay will be stationed along an abandoned route, such as where a Forest Hills trestle on Metropolitan Avenue bears a stone inscription of 1908. Fast-forwarding, late 2026 will mark the groundbreaking of The QueensWay’s construction, complete with community leaders driving shovels into the soil alongside a lush forested but long-neglected industrial backdrop for phase 1.

Enter the world of Forest Hills resident Karen Imas, a creative visionary and diverse government relations, public affairs, and stakeholder engagement professional in the public, private, and nonprofit sectors. She serves as Director of Climate and Resiliency Policy at the Office of the NYC Comptroller. She once managed external affairs policy at Attentive Energy, which focused on clean energy, and was previously the program and policy lead with Waterfront Alliance. At CMW Strategies, she represented land use, infrastructure, and nonprofit clients. Above all, she has Queens communities and their future at heart.

The QueensWay will bridge Central and Southern Queens communities including Rego Park, Forest Hills, Woodhaven, Glendale, Richmond Hill, and Ozone Park, and also anchor Queens enthusiasts through recreation, the arts, cultural foods, and historic and environmental preservation. It also bridges historically disconnected residential areas. A much-needed green space will feature current and new diverse trees, native vegetation, and edible gardens. A pedestrian and bike path will offer a newly commanding bird’s-eye exposure of neighborhoods, and enable access to nearby bike lanes en route to Rockaway Beach and Jamaica Bay’s recreational spaces, as well as five subway lines, numerous commercial corridors, and schools.

Imas shared an abundance of benefits. “New public parkland will add crucial green space in neighborhoods that are underserved, particularly south of Forest Park. The QueensWay will create safe, dedicated biking and walking trails connecting neighborhoods from Forest Hills to Ozone Park. We will expand access to natural areas, linking directly into Forest Park. Tree canopies and green infrastructure will address flood mitigations. Public health benefits pertain to the active lifestyles of walking, running, and cycling for the nearly 250,000 residents living within a 20-minute walk. The QueensWay will offer alternative walking and biking routes to local schools and transit hubs. Economically, the QueensWay will boost foot traffic for neighborhood restaurants and immigrant-owned small businesses.”

QueensWay from Forest Park. Photo by Michael Perlman.

A wide range of recreation, activities, and special events will undoubtedly continue to evolve. Opportunities will also pertain to designated public spaces for performances and live music, community gatherings, public art, games, and movie screenings. “There will also be opportunities for cultural programming that celebrates the extraordinary diversity of Queens, along with environmental education, nature programming, and activities connected to the corridor’s native plants and wildlife. The goal is to create a place that is active year-round and gives different communities and generations many reasons to enjoy the QueensWay,” said Imas.

It all began in 2011, when Queens residents living alongside the abandoned LIRR Rockaway Beach Branch had an ambitious vision, joined forces, and began advocating for its revitalization into a vibrant yet serene public park. Imas reminisced, “This grassroots effort led to the creation of Friends of the QueensWay, a community-driven organization supported by hundreds of individuals and groups through petitions, fundraisers, cleanups, tours, and events. Their shared vision was to reimagine this 3.5-mile stretch as a thriving greenway for walkers, joggers, cyclists, and visitors from Queens and beyond.”

Friends of the QueensWay partnered with Trust for Public Land to engage the community by gathering feedback, and develop a plan to transform 47 acres into a green space that consolidates neighborhoods while boosting economic and cultural growth. “What began as a grassroots vision evolved for more than a decade into a community-supported, city-backed project. The vision has been shaped by hundreds of conversations with residents, community organizations, elected officials, and other stakeholders, ultimately bringing the QueensWay from an idea to a project moving towards construction this fall,” explained Imas.

The dynamic development team consists of Techno + Sasaki for design and engineering, the NYC Economic Development Corporation, and NYC Parks. Friends of the QueensWay staff and board members reside in communities along the QueensWay, and consist of inaugural executive director John Surico, Karen Imas, Ruben Ramales, Travis Terry, Andrea Crawford, Doug McPherson, Allison Sesso, and Sharon Levy.

Between fall 2022 and 2026, the city announced over $50,000,000 in funding to complete the design and construction of the QueensWay’s Metropolitan Hub segment. “The intent of this section, which stretches from Metropolitan Avenue to Union Turnpike and spans 0.3 miles, is to build phase 1 of the new greenway adjacent to the Metropolitan Expeditionary Learning School,” said Imas.

Throughout the 15-year community initiative, Friends of the QueensWay developed an active steering committee of local residents and volunteers, and hosted over 150 engagement events, tours, and informational sessions throughout Central Queens, alongside partners from the Trust for Public Land. Thousands of residents were engaged in a community dialogue. In 2023, the EDC and NYC Parks held virtual sessions, where community feedback was compiled to prioritize the design and programming.

Imas explained, “We hosted educational walks and classroom sessions with Metropolitan Expeditionary Learning School students, site tours with planners, architects, and environmental organizations, bike tours around the vicinity of the QueensWay with cycling enthusiasts, tabling with local business owners at street fairs, and importantly, public cleanups, walking tours, and information sessions.” One must wonder if artifacts have been uncovered, and in fact, the corridor harbors substantial railroad-era remnants, such as fragments of former stations and the rails. More treasures are bound to be excavated as construction commences. However, most uncovered items are illegally dumped car parts, tires, and electronics.

Volunteer opportunities are plentiful and can be found on the QueensWay’s social media and Trust For Public Land’s website. An upcoming public cleanup of the QueensWay in Forest Park will be held on September 27 at 10:30 AM (meet at Stop & Shop), and The QueensWay 5K 2026 will be on October 4 at 9 AM at Victory Field.

Elected officials provided QueensWay endorsements, and Queenswide supporter organizations include Trust for Public Land, Queens Tourism Council, Queens Chamber of Commerce, Forest Hills Crescent Civic Association, Regional Plan Association, Forest Hills Youth Athletic Association, Indo-Caribbean Alliance, Richmond Hill Historical Society, Rails-to-Trails Conservancy, New Yorkers for Parks, Transportation Alternatives, Metro Village of Forest Hills, New York League of Conservation Voters, Association for a Better New York, Citizens Committee for NYC, Ridgewood Glendale Little League, Center for an Urban Future, Rajkumari Cultural Center, Center for Active Design, Queens Distance Runners, and Earth Citizens Club of Queens NY.

Historical knowledge and features along an abandoned train line grant public inspiration and offer a behind-the-scenes spirit that presents a story to the modern eye. It has been 64 years since abandonment, which builds upon its early twentieth century origins. “Trees sprouted and matured along the former right-of-way, creating a dense canopy and a diverse habitat for birds and other wildlife,” said Imas. However, abandonment poses several cons. She continued, “With little management, illegal dumping is an increasing problem. Trash and remnants of drug and alcohol use litter the ground. Degraded soil and invasive vegetation of railway embankments allow stormwater to flood adjacent homes and backyards. Many people are unaware of this hidden stretch of trees and dense undergrowth intermingling with the old rails, with viaduct bridges at road crossings providing the rare clue to the 3.5-mile path stretching from Rego Park to Ozone Park.”

With every great project, as time has proven, some members disagree or lack confidence in the QueensWay, and therefore, the planners have been very mindful. “We take public feedback seriously and recognize that people have legitimate questions about privacy, property impacts, maintenance, access, and the future of the corridor. Our approach is to listen, understand specific concerns, and determine whether it can be addressed through design, operations, or additional information,” said Imas. “Community engagement is not just about promoting the QueensWay, but rather an opportunity to improve the project and ensure a transparent process. Our responsibility is for those affected to have a meaningful opportunity to be heard, and their concerns receive a substantive response.”

Residents ask questions about the potential for crime and raised concerns about cleanliness, but Imas and her colleagues ensure safety and cleanliness as a fundamental towards the QueensWay’s success. “The design incorporates clear sightlines, lighting, multiple access points, and active public spaces to create a well-used, visible environment. Currently, NYC Parks among our city will be responsible for ongoing maintenance and security,” said Imas. “We also envision strong community stewardship, with residents and local organizations keeping the corridor clean and cared for. A place that is active, visible, and maintained is more likely to feel safe and welcoming to everyone who uses it.”

Furthermore, decades of empirical evidence signify that converting abandoned, overgrown rail corridors into managed public pathways consistently decreases illicit activity. Countrywide, greenway and rails-to-trails models have a longstanding track record of success, transforming abandoned industrial corridors into vibrant, beautiful, and memorable public destinations that offer measurable economic, environmental, and public health benefits. As trees and flowers blossom, personal relationships have too.

A cleanup & tour of the planned QueensWay’s Forest Park ravine area. Courtesy of Friends of the QueensWay.

Residents will also develop a multi-level relationship with nature. Core design elements are a rich collection of native plants, shrubby understory providing important habitat, and a trail shaded by a light canopy of trees and biodiversity/ecological restoration. For the several decades of abandonment, trees sprouted and matured, creating a dense canopy and a diverse habitat for birds and wildlife. However, invasive plants constricted native tree species. Ailanthus, poison ivy, and Japanese knotweed will be addressed. Imas explained, “Tree canopy and vegetation is critical green infrastructure in flood-prone Central Queens. This project can also be an important piece of neighborhood flood resilience. The existing railroad embankments have degraded soils and vegetation that contribute to runoff into neighboring properties. The project will restore native vegetation, stabilize embankments, and incorporate rain gardens, bioswales, and other green infrastructure to capture and slow stormwater.”

A renewed respect for wildlife awaits, as The QueensWay is destined to become a living laboratory for urban biodiversity. “The project is restoring a native habitat that can support birds, butterflies, and pollinators along the Atlantic Flyway. Since the corridor runs alongside schools, there’s an opportunity for students to monitor that biodiversity, and observe how the ecosystem changes over time,” said Imas.

Small business partnerships bear much potential, and are already underway. Imas and her team feels incredibly excited about the prospects for such activity and economic development across the Metropolitan Avenue corridor as the launching point. “Friends of the QueensWay built a relationship with the Queens Chamber of Commerce and Metro Village of Forest Hills, and looks forward to creating opportunities for small businesses to be more embedded in our project. Every $1 invested in parks and recreation generates at least $3 in annual local economic benefits, according to TPL’s 2026 analysis,” said Imas.

Besides preserving early twentieth century industrial relics that entail trestles and towers, the QueensWay fosters an opportunity for creative decor by planners, designers, and community artists including school students, and could offer a gallery ambiance. She explained, “We hope to create opportunities for sculptures, murals, installations, and outdoor exhibits that respond to the bridges, rail infrastructure, landscape, and neighborhoods along the corridor. We would also love to see local schools, artists, and community organizations involved through art projects, competitions and rotating exhibitions, giving artists a platform and allowing the communities along the QueensWay to help shape its identity.”

When the QueensWay’s key parties are not focusing on the initiative, they are pursuing a multitude of interests, although the QueensWay can be a time-consuming labor of love. Imas explained, “We are local parents and residents, as well as volunteers and leaders in youth, civic, religious, cultural, and community organizations throughout Queens. Our board also includes people with expertise in housing and community development, health and human services, architecture and planning, government and public affairs, economic development, parks and open space, and more. What connects us is a shared view that the QueensWay can help address many characteristics our neighborhoods need more of, including safe and accessible open space, recreation, opportunities for young residents, environmental resilience, arts and culture, and stronger connections between communities. That diversity is one of the strengths of Friends of the QueensWay.”

In the short-term, Friends of the QueensWay looks forward to working with city partners and the Forest Park Trust to ensure that phase 1 is well maintained upon completion. In the long-term, the organization highly anticipates collaborating with the City of New York to secure further funding and advance plans for future phases.

Stay tuned for next week’s column, which will provide a first-hand, in-depth perspective at the QueensWay’s very first executive director, John Surico, who will share his background, vision, and goals.

Shopping for TikTok likes can look straightforward. A service lists a quantity, attaches a price, and invites the customer to submit a video link. Yet the package selection reveals only a fraction of what a buyer needs to understand. The more revealing questions concern responsibility. What exactly has the company agreed to deliver? How will progress be communicated? What happens if the total falls afterward? And which claims describe the transaction rather than its possible effect on a business? SocialWick, SocialAdmire, InstaBoost & Famety illustrate several ways these services are presented. Looking at them through practical purchasing questions creates a clearer comparison than treating every advertised feature as equally valuable.

SocialWick

SocialWick offers TikTok likes that can be ordered without supplying a password. Its broader service range also includes other social media products, while its stated customer provisions include 24-hour support and refill coverage.

For a prospective buyer, the support channel offers an opportunity to resolve uncertainties before money changes hands. Useful questions include which video details are required, what the delivery estimate covers, and how an incomplete order would be investigated. A support response should be specific enough to guide a decision. General reassurance provides little help if the customer still cannot determine when fulfillment should finish or which conditions govern a replacement.

SocialAdmire

SocialAdmire emphasizes lower-cost access to TikTok likes and related services. That positioning may attract buyers with a tightly defined spending allowance, but the final decision still depends on the complete offer. A practical comparison considers the required minimum purchase, anticipated delivery window, and available assistance. Any replacement conditions should be included in the assessment as well. A cheaper package may be less appealing if the customer cannot obtain a clear explanation of what happens after a problem.

InstaBoost

InstaBoost promotes a paced approach to delivery alongside password-free purchasing and refill protection. The outstanding question is how that pacing is determined. A customer may need to ask whether it follows a fixed schedule, changes with the order quantity, or allows any adjustment. The important distinction is between delivery behavior and audience behavior. Receiving likes in smaller increments does not show that people watched attentively, found the content useful, or intend to return. Descriptions such as “high quality” require similar care. Without a clear definition and supporting evidence, they remain promotional language.

Famety

Famety describes the ability to allocate likes across multiple videos. Before choosing that arrangement, a customer should confirm the permitted number of posts, any minimum allocation, and how the distribution is specified. Famety also describes its accounts as vetted and states that login passwords are unnecessary. Those claims concern the service’s presentation and ordering process. They do not establish that the accounts involved will develop an ongoing interest in the content.

Author Roland Mullaev, holding up Lucky, takes steps on a commendable anti-bullying journey, Photo by Michael Perlman.

Author Roland Mullaev’s book, “A Dog Named Lucky,” promotes an anti-bullying message. 

By Michael Perlman 

“My greatest goal is to make a lasting positive impact on children’s lives. If Lucky can help even one child feel more confident, supported, or brave during a difficult time, then the journey of creating this story is worthwhile,” said Roland Mullaev, a compassionate Rego Park resident and one-man dynamo who most recently authored a 20-page children’s book, “A Dog Named Lucky.”

At 40, Mullaev’s day job is serving Costco shoppers as manager, but despite a busy schedule, his productive vibes came forth by fulfilling his dream as an author. He was born in Coney Island and raised in Rego Park to parents who immigrated from Russia in 1977. He achieved a degree at LaGuardia Community College.

Mullaev’s dedication signifies a call for stewardship, and it can be said that besides being an anti-bullying advocate, he is an animal advocate. “This book is dedicated to all the dog owners out there in the world. Dogs are said to be man’s best friend, and they have proved it time and time again. So please, please, take good care of them in the best way possible.”

“A dog will teach you unconditional love. If you can have that in your life, things won’t be too bad” is a famed inspirational quote by actor Robert Wagner, which is referenced in Mullaev’s book.

In 2020, his interest in writing a children’s book originated from a desire to make a positive difference in the lives of children. In June 2026, his book was published through Crexton Publishers. The book was edited by this columnist and illustrated by Evelina Brozgul, a longtime friend of his family.

“I wanted to create a story that was not only entertaining, but carried a meaningful message about kindness, courage, and standing up to bullying,” said Mullaev. “I have always believed that books have the power to inspire young readers and help them navigate life’s challenges. That inspired me to create Lucky, a story about a remarkable dog who can fly and talk, and uses his unique abilities to protect children from bullying. My hope is that every child who reads Lucky will feel empowered, know they are not alone, and understand that they always have the strength to stand up for themselves and others.”

Mullaev’s major motivation for writing “Lucky” was to help children understand that bullying is never acceptable, and no one should feel alone when facing it. Achieving a story that focused on confidence, friendship, and advocacy was also part of his mission. He explained, “By creating a lovable and heroic dog like Lucky, I hoped to make these important lessons engaging and memorable for children. My goal is for every reader to finish the book, believing that even one act of courage or kindness can make a meaningful difference in someone’s life.”

Selecting the name “Lucky” and the breed is a story of abundant meaning. “I visualized the main character as a dog, since dogs are often seen as loyal, protective, and unconditionally loving companions. Those qualities made a dog the perfect hero for a story about helping children who are being bullied,” said Mullaev. Lucky is also simple, memorable, and symbolizes hope. “In my story, children are ‘lucky’ to have a friend like Lucky, but Lucky also reminds them that true courage comes from within,” he continued.

Mullaev selected the breed to reflect Lucky’s character, which consists of being friendly, approachable, intelligent, and brave. “I wanted children to immediately connect with him and view him as a trustworthy friend who is always willing to stand up for those who need help. Lucky represents the kind of companion every child would want by their side during difficult times.”

Author Roland Mullaev, holding up Lucky, takes steps on a commendable anti-bullying journey, Photo by Michael Perlman.

Mullaev witnessed bullying and comprehends the impact it can have on people, especially children. He explained, “Bullying can take many forms, including hurtful words, exclusion, teasing, and making someone feel like they do not belong. Seeing how deeply these experiences can affect a person’s confidence and emotional well-being helped inspire me to write ‘Lucky.’”

He believes every child deserves to feel valued, respected, and supported. “Through my book, I wanted to address the challenges that many children face and create a message of hope, reminding young readers that kindness, courage, and compassion can overcome negativity. My goal is to encourage children to speak up, support one another, and understand that they have the strength to make a difference.”

Mullaev shared a message for children among multi-generational people who are victimized often. He said, “For children who experience bullying, discrimination, or feel like they are being treated differently, they should always remember their self-worth. No child should ever feel ashamed of who they are, where they come from, or what makes them unique. Our differences are what make us special, and every person deserves to be treated with kindness and respect.”

He wants children to know that they are not alone and that it is essential to speak up, reach out to trusted adults, and support peers who may be experiencing similar struggles. “Small acts of kindness can have a powerful impact, and one person’s courage can inspire many others. Through Lucky, I hope to remind children that they have an inner strength that can help them overcome challenging moments. Just like Lucky stands up for children in my book, we all have the ability to stand up for ourselves, as well as for those who need a friend.”

By writing “Lucky,” Mullaev feels he has acquired the responsibility of becoming an anti-bullying advocate, and his goal is not only to share an entertaining story for children and their parents but also to generate awareness about the importance of kindness, empathy, and standing up for one another. He plans to fulfill his mission by focusing on sharing Lucky’s message with children, families, schools, and communities. He explained, “I hope to participate in school visits, book readings, and library and community events, and engage in conversations that encourage children to treat each other with respect and compassion. I want ‘Lucky’ to become more than just a book, but a reminder that every child has value and that everyone has the ability to make a positive difference. By reaching young readers and encouraging them to choose kindness over cruelty, I hope to help create a world where children feel safe, supported, and confident by being themselves.” He also visualizes forming a partnership with organizations that support children and anti-bullying initiatives.

Lucky bears the potential to become more than just a character between the pages. A physical representation could be symbolic of friendship, bravery, and hope. His book could be a catalyst for additional books, educational programs, and merchandise, and lessons in morals and values for even more young readers. Mullaev explained his vision. “Creating a larger-than-life Lucky figure, as well as a collectible heroic figure similar to classic action figures, would be an exciting way to bring the character into the real world, and enable children to connect with him in a new way. Lucky can become a character who reminds them that they are important and have a voice.”

Becoming a published author was marked by rewarding challenges. “One of the largest challenges was taking an idea that existed in my imagination and turning it into a complete book that could connect with children and families. Writing a story is only the beginning; bringing the characters to life, working on the editing process, finding the right illustrations, and preparing my book for readers all require patience, dedication, and attention to detail,” said Mullaev.

His humanitarian and creative spirit was also met with many pleasant surprises. “Seeing Lucky come to life through illustrations and hearing how the story connects with readers has been incredibly meaningful. Knowing that a character I created can inspire children, encourage kindness, and help start important conversations about bullying, has made my entire journey worthwhile.”

Mullaev also shared insights for younger generations who aspire to follow his path. “For young readers and aspiring writers, my message is to believe in your ideas, and never be afraid to share your imagination with the world. Every great story begins with a simple idea. Writing requires hard work and persistence, but if you are passionate about your story and believe in its message, you can turn your dream into a reality.”

There is much to be grateful for, beginning with the opportunity to share a story that has a meaningful purpose and the potential to make a difference in children’s lives. He explained, “I am thankful for the support and encouragement I received throughout my journey of creating Lucky, from developing the idea to bringing the character and an anti-bullying message to my readers. I am also grateful for my family, friends, and everyone who believed in my vision, and encouraged me to continue pursuing this dream. Their support helped me stay motivated through the challenges of writing and publishing.”

Most importantly, Mullaev is grateful for the ability to apply his creativity and spread a message of kindness, courage, and compassion. “Knowing that Lucky may help children feel less alone and inspire them to stand up for themselves and others is something I truly value,” he said.

When he is not writing or working, he values quality time with his family and seeking opportunities to remain connected with people who are close to him. He enjoys participating in activities that cultivate his creative nature, in addition to making new discoveries, and feeling inspired by the world around him. In his leisure time, he enjoys relaxing, exploring new ideas, and finding inspiration that he can apply to his creative work.

“I have always embraced the importance of kindness, helping others, and being involved in my community. Many experiences and conversations I had throughout my life influenced my writing, and helped shape the message behind ‘Lucky,’” said Mullaev. “Whether through personal experiences, observing the world around me, or sharing my time with others, I believe that everyday moments can lead to meaningful ideas and stories.”

Mullaev hopes that “Lucky” inspires children to be brave, speak up when something is wrong, and remember that they have the ability to make the world around them a better place. “My dream is for Lucky’s message to reach children everywhere, and remind them that kindness is one of the greatest strengths we can share.” Lucky may soon be coming to a street corner near you. Parents, teachers, children, and friends can purchase a signed copy of “Lucky” from the author by emailing Roland.Mullaev@gmail.com. Roland Mullaev is also available for scheduling at book talks and signings in public and private event settings, and his advocacy will continue to take wing.
