item.content:encoded:
Views: 126

The historic Rego Park recreation center is getting upgraded for the next generation.

By Michael Perlman 

Among the top ten questions from Rego Park and nearby residents is “When is Lost Battalion Hall Recreation Center reopening?” Their long-awaited wishes will soon be granted by the Parks Department, as the historic building at 93-29 Queens Boulevard will offer improved accommodations, and its doors will reopen this fall.

Back in October 2017, the design phase originated, and construction followed in July 2022. “The $25.9 million capital project included a renovation of the building entry and lobby, as well as renovations to the fitness and weightlifting facilities,” explained the NYC Parks Spokesperson. “The upgraded facility will now be fully accessible and in compliance with ADA standards, while safety systems and stairs have been upgraded. Important interior and exterior upgrades to deteriorated stormwater systems have been made, improving the facility’s drainage systems. The historic Works Progress Administration (WPA) murals were carefully covered and protected throughout the construction process.”

The project became a reality due to the teamwork of the designers, 1100 Architect, and D & S Restoration, Inc., the construction contractor. Construction concluded, and it will reopen after the NYC Parks Public Programs team sets up Lost Battalion Hall Recreation Center for public use, continuing a rich community tradition in Queens.

This historic site has served as a community beacon for nearly 90 years. From 1938 to 1939, the WPA funded an Art Moderne building for $100,000, which bears homage to the 77th Division of the U.S. Army for its heroism in the Battle of Argonne in France during WWI. Over half of its 550 American soldiers perished and are remembered as members of “The Lost Battalion.” The building was placed under Parks Department jurisdiction in 1960. It was adapted for the community as a recreation center for children to seniors with diverse programs and activities, including art, a media lab, weightlifting, ping-pong, basketball, and fitness classes.

Lost Battalion Hall, 1940, Courtesy of Historian Ron Marzlock.

Mayor Michael Bloomberg presented a proclamation and designated August 22, 2003 as “77th Appreciation Day” in recognition of the brave men and women who served on behalf of our nation. An excerpt read: “For 86 years, the 77th Army Infantry Division has protected our city and our nation in times of crisis. On its 86th anniversary, we salute its descendant, the 77th Army Reserve Command and its courageous and skilled members who continue this illustrious unit’s legacy of valor. The unit was established on August 25, 1917 in New York State, and was called the ‘Metropolitan Division’ because a large percentage of its membership was residents of New York City.”

Adorning the brick façade is a tributary limestone inscription with two bronze tablets of the Statue of Liberty. In a most unassuming place, the gymnasium, players encounter two “Sailor, Soldier, Marine” WPA murals of the Lost Battalion in action, which were painted in 1938 by influential American painter Oscar Julius (1882 – 1965), and underwent restoration in 1995. He pursued his studies at Boston Museum School, National Academy of Design, and Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts. Back in 1921, he was among the founders of the Guild of American Painters.

Two bronze plaques are displayed in the lobby. One features Lady Liberty with an inscription that reads, “In Memory of The Lost Battalion. Built AD 1938 By Work Projects Admin. George U. Harvey, Boro. President of Queens.” Another memorial plaque features Borough President Harvey’s portrait as Lieutenant colonel, DSC (Distinguished Service Cross) dedicated by the citizens of Queens in 1946.

Lost Battalion Hall memorial plaque, Photo by Michael Perlman.

Historically, the building featured a firing range and drill hall for the Queens Veterans of Foreign Wars and the American Legion. This is also where the Civilian Defense Volunteer Office welcomed enrollees for World War II. In 1941, 2,000 guests celebrated President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s birthday with a dance to aid an infantile paralysis drive. Helen Becker would play piano for the GIs with the United Service Organizations (USO) during WWII. Among other diverse events are square dance festivals in the 1940s, an appearance by professional basketball player Bobby McDermott in 1950, boxing matches, a Perquackey contest in 1966, and testimonials for President Truman and President Eisenhower. It also accommodated nursery school, senior programs, arts and crafts, and 1980s breakdancing. The hall was also referenced in the four-season televised sitcom “Dear John” starring Judd Hirsch circa 1989. Among the humanitarian causes the center participated in more recent years were food donations and joining forces with the Department of Homeless Services’ community outreach initiatives.

The January 6, 1943 edition of the Long Island Daily Press captured Lost Battalion’s vibe. It read, “Besides the Civilian Defense Volunteer Office, it houses the Veterans of Foreign Wars welfare bureau which occupies two rooms. Various dances, rallies, and meetings are held from time to time in the auditorium, and on Saturday nights amateur boxing bouts are staged. The CDVO in Queens is headed by Mrs. John Adikes of Jamaica Estates and Charles G. Meyer of Bayside. It acts as the recruiting agency, the manpower reservoir and the morale arm for the Office of Civilian Defense agencies in Queens.”

Lost Battalion Hall helped shape the career of basketball legend “New York No. 19” Willis Reed, who passed away on March 21, 2023, but will always be remembered as “The Captain.”

From 1964 to 1974, he played with the New York Knicks, and then served as a coach and vice president of basketball operations for the New Jersey Nets to senior vice president of basketball. His incredible journey resulted in becoming a Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame inductee in 1982, and being recognized as one of the “50 greatest players in NBA history” in 1996.

In the early 1970s, Reed resided nearby in a three-room apartment at the 61-35 98th Street building of Park City Estates, and could be spotted at Lost Battalion Hall, where the New York Knicks would practice.

Lost Battalion Hall boxing circa May 1962, Courtesy of the Parks Dept.

The recreation center harbors distinctive memories, as it has played a diverse role in the lives of residents near and afar. “My Russell Sage Junior High School and Forest Hills High School friends and I played basketball there many Saturdays in the late 1960s and early 1970s,” reminisced Irwin Curtin of Parsippany, New Jersey, who was raised in Princeton Gardens at 88-11 63rd Drive. “I remember occasionally seeing the Knicks’ Cazzie Russell, who lived nearby, practicing free throws.” Basketball player and coach Cazzie Russell is recognized as an NBA All-Star, and for winning an NBA Championship with the Knicks in 1970, among his other achievements. Another famed basketball player, who could be spotted weightlifting, was the late Harthorne Wingo, a New York Knicks 1973 Champion.

Florida resident Alan Feldstein, formerly of Forest Hills, reminisced, “In the late sixties, my friends and I used to watch the Knicks practice there. They were all very friendly. We mostly played basketball at Russell Sage because it was closer to where we lived, but every couple of weeks depending on the weather, we would go to Lost Battalion, since the competition was much better.” Besides crossing paths with Willis Reed and Cazzie Russell, they would see basketball player and former Senator Bill Bradley and basketball player Jerry Lucas.

Perry Russell, who graduated from Forest Hills High School in 1967, resided at 105-38 64th Road. He explained, “When we were young, going to the Lost Battalion was a big deal. It was serious balling. You would be playing alongside kids from other neighborhoods. It was a tough place to play. We never played on the main courts, since that’s where the college players and top high school kids were. When I came back from college, I was a little out of shape. Pete Gottshalk, Fred Rosenthal and I started going twice a week. Pete was our tall guy at 5 ft. 9 in, I was 5 ft. 7 in, and Fred was 5 ft. 6 in. Red Holzman of the Knicks hit the open-man kind of ball. After a few weeks, I was playing as well as ever. You went to the Battalion for real ball.”

“I played basketball and remember being in the locker room with Walter Jones ‘The Big Bell’ Bellamy (6 ft. 11 in) of the New York Knicks in the early 1960s. I also attended High Holiday services for the overflow of congregants from Rego Park Jewish Center,” explained Westchester resident Marty Fiedler, formerly of Princeton Gardens at 88-04 63rd Drive.

“My father, Morris Weissbrot, started the weightlifting program and ran many meets. I went there as a teen to square dancing around 1962, and my friends and I had a blast,” said Binnie Aquilino. She was raised in Brooklyn and resides in Flushing.

The community was a breeding ground for its neighborly spirit and influential figures in the arts and recreation, as reinforced by Lisa Reskakis Rodriguez, who would visit Lost Battalion Hall in the late 1960s. “We were practicing for an ‘Annie Get Your Gun’ production and had fun,” she recalled. It felt like a Friday tradition. “I lived in Park City until 1983 and moved to Wetherole Street, followed by Westchester in 1991. Sometimes we would see Willis Reed and Cazzie Russell walking up the path outside my terrace, since they lived in Park City Estates.”

Sunnyside resident Michael Cassara, president of the Metropolitan Postcard Club of New York City, explained one of many roles that Lost Battalion Hall played in politics. “When Covid hit in 2020, there was an anticipated shortage of Election Day poll-workers. I signed up, as did a number of friends, and Queens ended up having a surplus of worker options. A few hundred people were instructed to report to Lost Battalion by 5 AM on Election Day before awaiting a next assignment. I ran into people I hadn’t seen in months, and by 8 AM, they gave me a same-day assignment in Richmond Hill, but the energy at Lost Battalion was quite special that morning.”

WPA mural 2 by Oscar Julius, Photo by Michael Perlman, 2020.

Retired longtime Forest Hills High School teacher Patty Bugland of Forest Hills praised the center for its huge difference in the youth scene. “A number of former students from my I.S. 8 years used to take the Q60 there and back after school, on weekends, and during summers for whatever recreational activities they could.” Looking forward, she added, “I was hoping that the building would be restored, not destroyed or redesigned, since so many of our older buildings have been lost. An upgrade can keep a meaningful building largely intact while modernized.”

In 2020, Lost Battalion Hall Manager Angela Elie, who served the community since 2011, was interviewed by this columnist. “We engage people of all ages and abilities through art, music, technology, and so much more. I enjoy watching seniors get active through various programs,” she said.

Elie pointed out her diverse experiences, including working with professional basketball players. She said, “One of our former teen members plays for Oklahoma City Thunder and won the NBA All-Star Slam Dunk Contest in 2019. I felt a sense of pride watching the content and even told my husband, ‘That’s my kid!’” Other unforgettable moments included a holiday event with Derek Jeter portraying Santa Claus. “A most notable perk is that I get to work in a building with so much life, character, and history every day. I love meeting people that visit who are relatives of those that were part of the Battalion,” she said.

Square Dancing at Lost Battalion Hall, Courtesy of the Parks Dept.

In affiliation with her staff, she was noted for developing enrichment programming, including culinary arts. At the time, she explained, “This program is tailored for children ages 8 to 13, and helps them get comfortable in the kitchen. Participants prepare three-course meals inspired by international cuisines with the assistance of New York Cares volunteers. We also host a Study The Stars Program that actively explores the field of astronomy. Participants utilize our state-of-the-art telescopes on the rooftop, and are encouraged to engage with our natural environment.”

As of 2020, when the center’s youth coach Eric Friedman served for 25 years, he considered the historic building a second home. “Knowing that Lost Battalion Hall bears homage to the 77th division of the US Army makes me feel proud to be an American.” As the coordinator of tiny tot programs for ages 1 to 3, he said, “Watching children learn, grow, and develop is truly enriching. My programs teach and prepare toddlers for preschool, and it’s been a pleasure to work with families of the surrounding communities.” He was also recognized for coach street hockey and directing the afterschool program. “I tell all my athletes, members, and program participants to enjoy life and respect their families and communities. As long as they focus on that, they can always reach for the stars,” said Friedman.

He fondly recalled Derek Jeter’s holiday event. “Jeter handed out gifts to hundreds of children, and I can’t begin to describe the priceless expressions on their faces when he walked in.” Another highlight was hosting the New York Rangers during a street hockey clinic. He said, “The players were so receptive to the children, and truly engaged our members to help them master the sport of hockey. It was great to see children interact with these athletes.” He also explained, “A few Golden Glove fighters trained as part of our boxing program. We run an Olympic weightlifting competition and had a few NBA players that played here before their professional careers began.”

item.content:encoded:
Views: 119

Arturo O’Farrill, Ivan Renta, Raul Reyes, Vince Cherico, Takafumi Nikaido, Photo by Bob Dea

By Michael Perlman

Each summer, the historic George Seuffert, Sr. Bandshell, which debuted on June 15, 1924 in scenic Forest Park, becomes a magnet for sponsored concerts featuring music and dance spanning diverse genres, living up to Queens’ nickname as “The World’s Borough.” In more ways than one, it proves that quality time shared among multigenerational families, friends, young couples, and as a community is priceless.

As the sun set on July 23, the party was just beginning thanks to the musical brilliance of the Arturo O’Farrill Quintet starring pianist, bandleader, and composer Arturo O’Farrill, a six-time Grammy winner. The concert earned a memorable spot in the hearts and minds of attendees from nearby and afar, and reinforced Queens as an anchor on the Queens Jazz Trail map, where the borough’s role as a jazz center originated in 1923. The pictorial Queens-wide map features the “who’s who” of jazz legends, where some consist of Louis Armstrong, Tony Bennett, Lena Horne, Benny Goodman, Clarence Williams and Eva Taylor, Bix Beiderbecke, Dizzy Gillespie, Count Basie, Ella Fitzgerald, and Glenn Miller.

“Queens has one of the richest jazz histories in New York City, and it’s an honor to help keep that legacy alive right here in Forest Park,” said NYC Parks Forest and Highland Park Administrator Portia Dyrenforth. “The Queens Jazz Trail brings the borough’s incredible jazz history to life in a way that feels personal and immediate, right in the neighborhoods where these legends once lived. The George Seuffert, Sr. Bandshell has been part of this community for over a century, and it’s wonderful to see it filled with music again each summer. Arts and culture programming like this is exactly why we do this work, as it gives people a reason to gather, celebrate their history, and connect with their neighbors.”

Arturo O’Farrill, a native of Mexico City who was raised in NYC and resides in Putnam Valley, was very enthusiastic to perform in Queens and grateful to be recognized on the Jazz Trail concert series. In an interview, he graciously shared his concert experience, background, career pursuits, and goals. He explained, “As my wife and I were coming in, we were blown away by how beautiful that park is, and when we came upon the Bandshell, we were also blown away. It’s a very idyllic setting and a beautiful bandshell that’s very simple, and it is where beautiful people can gather to hear music. I discovered a new uncharted treasure in Queens.”

Arturo O’Farrill, Photo by Bob Dea

O’Farrill shared the highlights of his evening’s repertoire and its relevance. He played “Chinas y Criollas,” a much-loved piece composed by Rob Mounsey, an acclaimed keyboardist in pop and rock. “It’s about a famous attribute for NYC, which is the diversity. One of the most interesting proliferations about New York is its Chinese-Cuban restaurants, which I have seen throughout much of Queens. I wanted to pay tribute to this incredible population, which has a historical presence. There is also a large Chinatown in Havana. We are amplified when we are diverse,” said O’Farrill.

A highlight was “To Wisdom, the Prize,” which was composed by jazz pianist Larry, who was a member of Jerry González’s Fort Apache Band. “He is one of the real heroes and mentors of that meeting place between Latin and jazz,” said O’Farrill. Another memorable piece was “Picadillo” a composition by the late great Tito Puente. “I first heard it in the hands of composer and bandleader Eddie Palmieri. We lost him recently. I loved Eddie in a way that I don’t understand. He influenced me as a musician and a human being. In the past few months, we celebrated a street co-naming on 112th Street and Park Avenue in his honor, ‘Eddie Palmieri Way.’ I wanted to celebrate not just him, but the contribution that New York has made to Latin jazz.”

A very well-known piece was “Obsesion.” “Every Cuban, Puerto Rican, Latino person has heard it. It’s a standard. It is a lot of fun, since it is a Guaguancó, a really fast rhythm that people really love,” said O’Farrill in relation to the Cuban rumba subgenre.

He references himself as “The Bad Bunny of jazz.” “We play music from all over the Americas, such as Colombian and Peruvian. We played ‘Action and Reaction,’ which was composed by a wonderful and brilliant Brazilian saxophonist, Livio Almeida. I joke around a lot, since for a reaction, there is an equal and opposite reaction; the first law of physics, which is also true in social interaction of day to day life,” said O’Farrill.

A highlight was “In Whom I Am Well Pleased.” “This is one of my compositions that I love to play, since it speaks to my commitment as a student and an educator,” said O’Farrill. He is a music professor at The New School and takes great pride in achieving his Master’s from the Aaron Copland School of Music at Queens College, where his focus was jazz theory and composition. He has been refining the foundation for his students for 30+ years, and taught at nearly every CUNY institution visualized. “I’m really proud of CUNY and the fact that more Nobel Peace Prize winners have come from there than almost any other institution. My piece also speaks of my pride in musicians. Sometimes people don’t realize that there is often no employment. Musicians are incredibly enough people who have studied the equivalent of a doctoral degree, and enter a freelance field with no guarantees. Musicians are extraordinary heroes. I spent a lot of my life’s work shoring up young musicians, so they can continue the traditions that my father and I and my sons had the privilege of being a part of.”

Life becomes a continuous composition. In the 1940s and 1950s, his father, Chico O’Farrill, was an acclaimed composer, arranger, and conductor who played a significant role by integrating Afro Cuban rhythms into jazz. His wife is classical pianist Alison Deane, and they take pride in their two sons, Zack and Adam, who are musicians and collaborators. O’Farrill and his wife are High School of Music & Art alumni, and their sons are graduates of LaGuardia High School of Music and Art and Performing Arts.

At the Bandshell, O’Farrill played alongside Ivan Renta on tenor saxophone. “I feel he’s one of the greatest saxophonists in the world today. He played with a virtual ‘who’s who’ of jazz and Latin superstars,” said O’Farrill. Another member of the quintet was percussionist/conguero Takafumi Nikaido. “He is a gentleman of Japanese descent who plays with all the soul, power, and grace of an Afro Cuban,” he said. Also spotlighted was Vince Cherico, a drummer that O’Farrill has been working alongside for nearly 30 years. He explained, “I’ve performed on stage with him worldwide. He performs Afro Latin music in a very natural way. He comes from a long line of drummers.” Performer Raul Reyes is among the great bassists who descended from Cuba. “People don’t realize that Cuba has one of the highest levels of trained musicians in the world. It’s incredible how people who have generally been impoverished created such a rich history of education in the arts,” explained O’Farrill, who noted pianists, trumpet players, and bassists as a case in point.

Takafumi Nakaido on conga, Photo by Bob Dea

O’Farrill explained a particularly memorable moment of the evening. “A highlight was when I asked people to participate by learning patterns from each layer of drumming in the piece, ‘Picadillo.’ I broke up the audience into four groups. They not only participated with gusto, but got up and danced. I loved it when children also participated, since sometimes they’re uptight around adults, but they danced and felt the freedom. To see that many people dancing and enjoying that moment of unity, is certainly beyond words.” Referring to being given a rather short life, he said, “Our goal is to help bring dignity and joy to human beings, regardless of what they are experiencing.”

Advice was offered to aspiring young singers seeking a music career. He recalled life as a struggling musician with no guarantee. “The great actor Alan Cumming said it best when asked what it was like to receive a Tony Award: ‘If you don’t love your craft when you’re waiting on tables to support it, you won’t love it when you’re on stage accepting a Tony Award.’ Finding joy in the struggle is as important as finding joy in the reaping of the rewards of a career in music. Make as much joy in singing as you can before you get successful. If you understand that the joy happens because of your love of the craft, then you’ll be okay. Find the joy regardless of where you are at in your career.” Afterall, love and joy are what audiences respond to.

O’Farrill reminisced the origins of his musical journey, along with his influences, and is grateful that he was born into a musical household. “It was expected that I’d follow in my father’s footsteps. I had music lessons by the time I was six. When I was twelve, I discovered my father’s record collection and pulled out a recording by (trumpeter and bandleader) Miles Davis, and fell madly in love with Herbie Hancock, who was playing on the record. From that point on I was smitten, and could see no other life for myself.” His career unraveled in the decades that followed, and he reflected upon it by stating, “I figured out early in my life that the recipe for my happiness is to play music I love, with people I love, for people I love.”

Raul Reyes, Ivan Renta, Vince Cherico, Photo by Bob Dea

O’Farrill owes gratitude to avant-garde jazz legend and composer Carla Bley for discovering him, with whom he spent years traveling. A big break transpired when he was approached by artistic director Wynton Marsalis to create an orchestra for Jazz at Lincoln Center as of 2002, leading to the launch of the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra. “I was lucky to discover a path towards consistently playing music for a living. I was blown apart with the idea that this joy could be expressed on the piano,” he said.

O’Farrill continues to share his gift as a creative visionary who developed Casa Belongó, a 20,000-square-foot state-of-the-art performance space, music education, preservation, and cultural hub in East Harlem, which broke ground in February.

Stepping behind the scenes, performances at the Bandshell materialize after a creative and proactive team effort. He explained, “You start writing grants months or years in advance, and you work with people who are really committed.” The Queens Jazz Trail series became a reality thanks to the Kupferberg Center for the Arts at Queens College, Flushing Town Hall, and the Louis Armstrong House Museum in partnership with NYC Parks, and sponsors Howard Gilman Foundation, Resorts World NYC, Northwell Health, Maspeth Federal Savings, and AARP New York.

O’Farrill feels inspired by the Queens Jazz Trail and said, “There’s a magic in the water in that part of the world that produces great musicians, festivals, and people, and wonderful parks. I have to be a good steward of the privilege of being part of the Queens Jazz Trail.” He linked the past to the recent past. “I remember visiting the Louis Armstrong House long before they built a center. I was profoundly impressed by the commitment that Louis Armstrong made to his neighborhood and Queens. There’s more than money at the beginning of these ventures. There’s a dream and an art commitment. What I loved about this particular concert was the connection to community. Queens has a history of incredible jazz musicians from there, living there, and returning.” Besides historic figures, he referenced contemporary greats such as electric bassist and composer Marcus Miller, and jazz and fusion drummer and composer Omar Hakim, with whom he had the pleasure to perform.

Looking out from the Bandshell into the audience in scenic Forest Park, Photo by Bob Dea

O’Farrill hopes to continue entertaining audiences throughout Queens. “I would be thrilled to perform at Forest Hills Stadium,” he said. On the horizon is “Spirits from Both Sides: Arturo O’Farrill x Vincent Hsu” on August 15 at 8 PM at Flushing Town Hall, a concert that he is particularly proud of. He and his band will collaborate with a Taiwanese musician. He explained, “We will be celebrating Afro Taiwanese and Afro Cuban Jazz. I spent much of my life exploring the global connections of culture. In my journey, I found out that the music we call jazz is a global experiment. It was brought here through a terrifying reality called slavery, but even that has exposure to cultural roots from the Middle East to the East Asia. People who were brought here against their will had influences from all over the world. The upcoming concert is a further expression of my belief that we are globally connected as a human race. We rise together.”

by John Sanchez

__

Montoya’s is quickly becoming one of Forest Hills’ newest neighborhood favorites, and now, the restaurant’s growing buzz has made its way to television.

Recently, Montoya’s partners Chef Jaime Montoya and Rob Salameh, along with Chief Brand Officer Jaclyn Burke, appeared together on FOX 5 New York’s “6 O’Clock Somewhere” segment, giving viewers a closer look at the restaurant, its food and the team behind its rapid rise in the local dining scene.

For the Montoya’s team, the appearance marked another exciting milestone for a restaurant that has quickly started to feel like a neighborhood staple.

“It’s incredibly rewarding to see the community embrace Montoya’s the way they have,” said Chef Jaime Montoya. “We wanted to create a restaurant where people could come for great food, stay for a drink and feel like they’re part of something. The response from Forest Hills has been amazing.”

Rob Salameh, a longtime local business owner, knows firsthand what it means to build a business in the community.

“Our guests have really become part of the Montoya’s family,” Salameh said. “Being a local business owner, I understand how important it is to build trust with the people in your community. Our customers are coming back, bringing friends and telling people about us. That kind of word-of-mouth is something you can’t manufacture. It’s happening naturally, and we’re extremely grateful for it.”

There may also be a little neighborhood mystery behind how Montoya’s ended up in front of the FOX 5 cameras.

One local resident and regular Montoya’s patron named Max, who happens to work at FOX 5, helped make the connection. We’ll leave the details there — but sometimes the best introductions come from the people sitting right at your table.

The timing couldn’t be better for Montoya’s. In a short period, the restaurant has developed a following among Forest Hills residents looking for Mexican cuisine, creative cocktails and a welcoming place to gather. Its inviting atmosphere and backyard patio have added to its appeal, giving locals another reason to stick around after dinner.

The menu is another major draw, featuring an assortment of specials that showcase the restaurant’s take on Mexican-inspired flavors. Highlights include the Mexican Shrimp Cocktail, Camarones Montoya — sautéed shrimp prepared with white wine, garlic and lemon — the Roasted Poblano Burger and a hearty Pork Chop special.

The bar has also become an important part of the Montoya’s experience. Guests can cool off with Tio Charlie’s Famous Frozen Sangria or try the Montoya Mojito, made with fresh-squeezed lime juice, fresh mint and homemade simple syrup.

Beyond the food and drinks, Montoya’s is also preparing to add a new piece of art to the restaurant through an upcoming mural project led by Burke. The mural has already generated excitement throughout the Forest Hills community, with residents showing their support for the project and anticipation for its completion.

“I’m excited to announce my upcoming mural at Montoya’s,” Burke said. “There has been so much support and excitement from the community surrounding this project, and I’m truly grateful for the opportunity to create something meaningful for the space. With the recent attention from FOX and other media, it’s been amazing to see the growing interest and support for what’s to come.”

For Burke, the restaurant’s quick connection with the community is exactly what makes the Montoya’s story stand out.

“Building a brand is about creating something people genuinely want to be part of,” Burke said. “Montoya’s has that energy. The food, the hospitality, the atmosphere and the people behind it are all coming together in a way that feels very authentic to Forest Hills.”

That authenticity may be the secret to Montoya’s rapid rise.

In a neighborhood filled with established restaurants and longtime favorites, becoming a true local staple is no small accomplishment. But with regulars filling the tables, new customers discovering the restaurant, an upcoming mural bringing another creative element to the space and now a FOX 5 appearance putting Montoya’s in front of an even wider audience, the restaurant appears to be well on its way.

And if the neighborhood response is any indication, Montoya’s may have gone from new restaurant to Forest Hills favorite faster than anyone expected.

Montoya’s is located at 102-15 Metropolitan Ave. in Forest Hills.

Observance cast & crew at world premiere.

By Michael Perlman

Forest Hills is a magnet for culture, art, architecture, and history, with iconic sites such as the Art Moderne Midway Theatre, home of the 10th annual Festival of Cinema NYC. Over 100 independent feature and short-length films spanning diverse genres, as well as music videos and web and TV episodic projects will be in the spotlight from August 7 to August 16. Additionally, Forest Hills Library will be the setting of complimentary film workshops and seminars, further engaging attendees. The mastermind behind Queens’ growing tradition is Jayson Simba, who was born in Woodside and raised in Forest Hills. The festival even earned a spot in Monopoly Queens Edition.

“What makes us unique is our effort to really connect with our community and our dedication to helping artists and filmmakers further their aspirations,” said Simba. “While other film festivals focus on the glitz and glamour of what they offer and who they are, Festival of Cinema NYC makes it a point to seek out and partner with other organizations that can offer opportunities beyond our capabilities.”

Narrow in on Forest Hills’-own Elyssa Nicole Trust, a 30-plus-year-old professional actress, playwright, screenwriter, voiceover artist, and children’s book author, who is employed by an ad agency. She attended Binghamton University, where she pursued English and Spanish with a concentration in journalism. Her indie TV pilot “Observance” is nominated for Best Episodic and Best Cinematography. She is not only the writer and producer, but stars in this distinctive work of art, which screens Saturday, August 8 at 3 PM at the Midway Theatre. “It feels amazing to be part of the Festival of Cinema NYC. It is incredibly special to share the pilot in my home city, and this time right here in Queens, where we shot most of it,” she said. Additionally, portions were filmed in Long Island, where she was raised.

“Screening in my own neighborhood at my local movie theater makes the experience especially meaningful. Every festival selection, award nomination, connection, and opportunity to show the pilot moves the project and my career forward, and I am ecstatic,” she continued. After spending seven years in Manhattan and five years in Brooklyn, she planted roots in Forest Hills over a year ago. She resides with her family, which includes her preschool-aged daughter and a Maltipoo.

“Observance” follows Gabby, a hard-partying secular Jew, whose life takes an unanticipated turn after a profound loss. “As she navigates grief and questions of identity, she embarks upon a transformative journey of self-discovery and spiritual renewal, ultimately becoming a Ba’alat Teshuvah, a previously non-observant Jewish woman who newly embraces a traditionally observant life,” said Trust.

“My hope is that the pilot resonates with audiences today and for generations to come,” said Trust, referencing “Observance” that offers a nuanced portrayal of the Jewish experience and humanizes Jewish people spanning all backgrounds. The timing of its release is most significant, and it aims to shed a “Let there be light” experience. Trust explained, “The film takes an empathetic approach to observant and secular Judaism, and signifies the vital role that women play in Jewish life. The script is intentionally sympathetic toward observant Jews at a time when religious Jewish communities are often depicted negatively in film and literature. There are significantly more stories about people looking to leave religious communities than stories about those choosing to join them, and we frequently see heartbreaking portrayals of intolerable behavior within these communities, particularly toward women. ‘Observance’ offers a favorable portrayal of Judaism in all forms and explores why a woman might find meaning, healing, and joy in becoming more observant.”

Trust, who along with her team engaged their heart on creating “Observance,” feels that being nominated is incredibly validating. The original stage rendition of “Observance” was the recipient of several award nominations. Earlier this summer, she was nominated for Best Actress at the Wyoming International Film Festival, which she views as super exciting. In reference to this season’s Festival of Cinema NYC, she said, “Seeing the work recognized in front of and behind the camera is truly humbling.”

Stepping behind the scenes, Trust was proud to share her film’s incredibly rewarding and challenging experience. She explained, “We assembled an amazing cast, and bringing this story of Jewish joy and identity to life with an all-Jewish cast and a Jewish female-led creative team was truly special. We created an ambitious, professional pilot on a crowdfunded independent budget, which required an enormous amount of resourcefulness. We also faced one obstacle after another, such as a Covid outbreak on set causing us to lose our entire art department for the final shoot day. After we wrapped, we discovered that footage from a memory card was accidentally recorded over, so we organized an additional pickup day and reshot seven scenes.”

The production process demanded consistent problem-solving, adaptability, and determination. “Audiences view the finished pilot, but may not realize how much persistence goes into creating independent work at this level. I developed the script over three years, and continued refining it almost daily in the months leading up to production,” she continued.

The Midway Theatre, which opened in 1942, was named after WWII’s Battle of Midway and designed by America’s foremost theater architect Thomas Lamb, along with consulting architect S. Charles Lee. “The festival has such a warm, community-centered ambiance, and it feels incredibly special to screen ‘Observance’ at the historic Midway Theatre, Thomas Lamb’s final theater, and such a meaningful Queens landmark,” said Trust. “Knowing that we’ll be sharing the film in one of the few surviving examples of his Art Moderne work gives the screening an added sense of occasion.”

“Observance” is a screen project that she expresses the greatest pride in, and values as the culmination of years of writing, development, producing, and performance. She is also proud of her web series based on her college a cappella group, as well as two short films she wrote and filmed last year. Her body of work also consists of several plays, including the original stage version of “Observance,” and her children’s book, “Daisy Moves to America.” “I take pride in creating across mediums and finding the form that best serves each story,” said Trust.

Elyssa Nicole Trust with her book, Daisy Moves to America, Photo by Mari Uchida.

Backtracking, Trust has been a storyteller for as long as she can recall, and “Observance” consolidates what she values as one; layered Jewish representation, complex female characters, and an exploration of grief, growth, and identity. She reminisced, “I caught the acting bug at eight when I performed in a camp production of ‘The Wizard of Oz,’ and I grew up pursuing musical theater. I’ve also been writing since age six. I wrote my first book in the first grade, so studying English in college was a natural choice.” After college graduation, she pursued freelance journalism and acting, but felt increasingly drawn to creative writing. That was when she began writing plays and screenplays to share the stories within her heart, and to create meaningful roles for her theater community and on a personal level. “I studied playwriting and screenwriting with brilliant teachers in New York City, and built a strong creative community along the way,” she proudly recalled.

She then explained, “Producing became a natural extension of my work as a writer and actor. I wanted to take artistic ownership of my projects, and make sure the stories I wrote actually made it from the page to the stage and screen. To me, film production is about a group of passionate, creative people bringing their individual talents together in service of a meaningful story. I love being on set, just as I love being onstage. It’s where I feel most like myself by being free, present, and alive!”

Trust owes much gratitude to her professional influences, who helped shape her career path. They include female showrunners and creators such as Tina Fey, Mindy Kaling, Shonda Rhimes, Phoebe Waller-Bridge, and Issa Rae. “I am especially inspired by Catherine Reitman, who created, executive produced, and starred in ‘Workin’ Moms.’ She built an entire series around women juggling love, careers, identity, and parenthood,” she said.

Rachel Bloom is also a major inspiration. “As a Jewish writer and performer who co-created, executive produced, and starred in ‘Crazy Ex-Girlfriend,’ she created a role and a world that were funny, specific, emotionally complex, and entirely her own.”

She considers Lena Dunham a genius. “She is only a little older than I am, and when I was in college, I saw what she was doing with ‘Girls,’ and realized it was possible to write, act in, and shape your own work.” Inspiration is also drawn from playwrights such as Bess Wohl, Lynn Nottage, and Lauren Gunderson.

Trust explained, “The throughline for me is women who create complex female characters, generate opportunities for themselves and other artists, and use writing as a vehicle for their other creative gifts. Their careers showed me that I did not have to choose between being an actor, writer, and creator, but I could build a career that included all three.”

Trust offered advice for younger generations hoping to cultivate their talents and pursue her career path. “Call yourself what you are. If you write, you are a writer, not an aspiring writer. If you play music, you are a musician, not an aspiring musician. Words matter. Tell the story that is in your heart, and don’t wait for permission from gatekeepers. Share your work, find artistic communities, and if you don’t have a support system, build one. It is really difficult to build a career in the entertainment industry without support.”

She also encourages young artists to think practically about building a sustainable career. “Creative careers can take many forms, and income can fluctuate, particularly as you are building momentum. Having multiple income streams can give you the stability and freedom to continue producing the work you care about,” said Trust.

In the short-term, she and her team plan to continue screening “Observance” at festivals to engage new audiences. As for the long-term, they aim to produce the full series and sell it to a streaming platform. Additionally, she plans to continue expanding her body of work as an actress, writer, and producer, while developing other original projects for the stage and screen.

“Observance” is only the beginning of Trust’s vision, since she intends to follow her heart by continuing her production journey through works that celebrate Jewish identity without apology, center women with agency, and offer audiences perspectives they may not have encountered. “As antisemitism continues to rise, and many Jewish people feel pressured to hide parts of themselves, I believe it is more important than ever to tell stories that present Jewish identity as a source of joy, connection, meaning, and pride,” said Trust.
